cases.abstract: DreamBooth personalizes a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model from three to five images, preserving a subject's identity across new contexts and poses. Fine-tuning associates a rare-token identifier with the subject and its class, drawing on the class prior to generate variations beyond the observed views. A prior-preservation loss uses class-only prompts and images generated by the original model to counteract collapse of the class into the personalized instance. We release an evaluation suite of 30 subjects and 25 prompts per subject, with a DINO-based metric for distinguishing individuals within a class. With Stable Diffusion for both methods, DreamBooth exceeds Textual Inversion in DINO similarity (0.668 versus 0.569) and text-image CLIP similarity (0.305 versus 0.255). Together with majority-vote human preferences of 68% for subject fidelity and 81% for prompt fidelity, these comparisons support retaining identity while responding to new descriptions. Imagen ablations show that prior preservation reduces class collapse and increases diversity, but slightly lowers subject fidelity. Qualitative examples show artistic renditions, novel views, and property changes; context-appearance entanglement, overfitting, and hallucinated details limit identity preservation.
cases.notes: Complementary identity and prompt comparisons address whether personalization retains the particular subject while following new descriptions; human preferences connect metric gaps to perceived fidelity. The shared Stable Diffusion backbone bounds the comparison without implying matched adaptation budgets. Retained the public evaluation suite and within-class identity metric as co-contributions. Imagen ablations support the regularizer's tested diversity and class-preservation role, not a guarantee of identity fidelity or an isolated explanation for every gain.

cases.abstract: Toolformer learns tool-use decisions through self-supervised language modeling, using a few demonstrations per tool. Candidate calls are executed and retained when their responses improve subsequent token prediction over both no-call and call-only alternatives; fine-tuning on augmented text teaches tool selection, argument generation, and response incorporation. Experiments use GPT-J and five text-based APIs in prompted zero-shot evaluation with at most one call per input. On ASDiv, accuracy is 40.4%, versus 9.6% after fine-tuning on the same text without calls and 14.8% with Toolformer's calls disabled, supporting useful tool access beyond further training alone. This exceeds GPT-3 (175B) at 14.0%, whereas question answering improves over GPT-J controls but remains below GPT-3. Factual completion and temporal benchmarks improve; translation calls help across evaluated languages without consistently surpassing unmodified GPT-J. With calls disabled, perplexity matches text-only fine-tuning on both evaluated corpora. In a three-tool GPT-2 sweep, useful tool use appears near 775M parameters, with search an exception; stronger base models can diminish weaker tools' utility. Independent call generation leaves chained and interactive use unsupported, limiting the evidence to noninteractive tool access.
cases.notes: Loss filtering makes tool responses, rather than call formatting alone, the self-generated training signal. The ASDiv text-only control holds corpus content fixed; disabling calls in the trained model separates inference-time tool access from training gains. GPT-3 is a larger external comparator, not a matched training control. Kept mixed QA and multilingual outcomes, the three-tool scaling scope, and the one-call/noninteractive boundary. Perplexity parity concerns disabled calls versus text-only fine-tuning; task scores retain the source's permissive answer criteria, not exact match.
